outcome: Basak, Dong, Saettone & Zaharescu (Univ. of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, with Zaharescu also at the Simion Stoilow Institute) proved corrected, sharp versions of Pollock's 1843 icosahedral and dodecahedral numbers conjectures — every positive integer is a sum of at most 15 icosahedral numbers (not Pollock's original 13) and at most 22 dodecahedral numbers (not Pollock's original 21) — via the Hardy-Littlewood circle method, Hasse-Weil bounds, Bombieri's exponential-sum theorem, and complete numerical verification of remaining small cases. This settles two of the several conjectures grouped under the 'Pollock's conjectures' bullet; the tetrahedral-numbers conjecture (241 exceptions, 343,867 conjectured largest) remains fully open, and the octahedral-numbers conjecture remains proved only for sufficiently large integers (Elessar Brady, 2016, predates the window).

counterexample.object: Specific integers refuting Pollock's original bound claims: for icosahedral numbers, 47, 83, 94, and 119 each require 14 icosahedral numbers (exceeding Pollock's claimed 13), and 95 requires 15; for dodecahedral numbers, 79 requires 22 dodecahedral numbers (exceeding Pollock's claimed 21), e.g. 79 = 20+20+20+1+1+...+1 with nineteen 1's.
counterexample.verified_how: Direct arithmetic verification of the polyhedral-number representations of these specific integers, combined with a computational search establishing no larger integer needs more terms; the corrected bounds (15, 22) were then proved sharp and universal via analytic number theory plus complete numerical verification for remaining bounded cases.

summary: The 'Pollock's conjectures' bullet groups five distinct claims by Frederick Pollock (1843/1850): sums of at most 5 tetrahedral, 7 octahedral, 13 icosahedral, 21 dodecahedral, or 9 cube numbers. Since 26 January 2024, the icosahedral and dodecahedral cases were fully settled by Basak, Dong, Saettone & Zaharescu (International Mathematics Research Notices, Vol. 2025, Issue 13, published within the window; a corresponding arXiv preprint 2608.08019 was posted 8 Aug 2026, i.e. after the journal publication, and I use the earlier journal date per §6.3's 'first public written argument' rule since it precedes the preprint here). The paper is a clean, expert-published resolution using the circle method, Hasse-Weil bounds, Bombieri's theorem, and computational verification of finitely many remaining cases — this counts as 'resolved' for the icosahedral/dodecahedral sub-cases individually, but I classify the overall bullet as 'partial' because the tetrahedral and octahedral sub-conjectures (also part of the same Wikipedia bullet) remain open or only asymptotically resolved, with no change to those since the window began. The result is 'mixed' in direction: it refutes Pollock's original numerical bounds (13, 21) — with explicit counterexamples 47/83/94/95/119 and 79 — while confirming corrected, sharp replacement bounds (15, 22). No AI system was involved anywhere in this work; the methods are entirely classical analytic number theory plus ordinary computational/numerical verification (e.g. the companion GitHub repository runs a plain Python brute-force check over stated integer ranges), which does not qualify as an AI system under §6.2. I found no acknowledgements, author statements, or secondary coverage mentioning any AI or machine-learning tool in connection with this result.
competing_reading: One could argue the bullet should be scored per-sub-conjecture rather than as one whole, which would make the icosahedral/dodecahedral portion 'resolved' outright; I chose 'partial' because Wikipedia presents all five claims under a single 'Pollock's conjectures' heading and the tetrahedral/octahedral cases are unresolved, so a careful reader of the whole entry would still find open content. Also arguable: the exact first-public-date is ambiguous given the arXiv preprint (Aug 2026) postdates the journal issue (Jul 2025) — an unusual ordering — so I used the earlier, journal date as the operative event date.
what_would_settle_it: A statement from the authors or arXiv moderation explaining why the arXiv posting (2608.08019, Aug 2026) came more than a year after the IMRN publication (Jul 2025) would resolve the dating ambiguity, though it doesn't change which is earlier. Resolution of the tetrahedral or octahedral sub-conjectures would change the overall bullet's status further.

judgement.doubts: Agree with the record. The bullet groups several Pollock conjectures (tetrahedral, octahedral, icosahedral, dodecahedral, cube); settling two is a case (F2), and IMRN acceptance makes it digested. Two doubts. (1) Direction: the paper's title says 'Proof of Pollock's Conjectures', but the record says it refutes Pollock's original bounds of 13 and 21 with small explicit integers. If those integers were known exceptions before the snapshot, or if the conjectures as usually stated already allowed them, the direction would be 'confirmed' and the counterexample flag would describe old computation, not this event. I left the record's reading in place because it gives specific integers. (2) Dating: the arXiv 2608.08019 posting comes after the July 2025 journal issue. Both dates are after the snapshot, so the status does not change.
